# Reproducible Research {#sec-reproducible-research}

::: {.guiding-question}
Guiding question: **Could someone else reproduce my analysis?**
:::

In this area you will learn how to: document your analysis, combine code, text and
results in Quarto, organise and share your work using GitHub and make your analytical
process transparent and reproducible. This chapter leans more heavily on external open
resources than Chapters 1–4, because reproducibility is best learned by doing it in your
own project, not by working through another isolated exercise dataset.

::: {.callout-note}
## This module practises what it teaches
Everything you've read so far — text, code, figures — lives in a Quarto project, version
controlled on GitHub, released under CC-BY. Reproducibility isn't a separate add-on
skill here; it's the format the whole module is built in.
:::

## Why Reproducibility Matters

A result you cannot reproduce is a result no one — including future you — can fully
trust. In environmental science specifically, claims often feed into policy; being able
to show *exactly* how a number was produced, from raw download to final figure, is part
of the scientific claim itself, not an optional extra.

> *Analogy:* a recipe that only works because the cook "just knows" to add a pinch of an
> unlisted ingredient is not a reproducible recipe, however good the dish tastes. A
> reproducible analysis is a recipe precise enough that someone else, in a different
> kitchen, gets the same dish.

The FAIR principles, widely used in Open Science, capture this as a checklist for data
and code: **F**indable, **A**ccessible, **I**nteroperable, **R**eusable. A well-organised
Quarto + GitHub project addresses all four almost automatically.

## From Scripts to Literate Programming

A plain `.R` script separates code from explanation — comments help, but the reasoning
usually lives in your head or a separate document. **Literate programming** (the idea
behind Quarto and R Markdown before it) interleaves narrative text, code and the code's
*output* — tables, figures, model summaries — in a single document that renders to
HTML, PDF or a website. This entire module is one example; your final report and
dashboard should be another.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Get started with Quarto
The official [Quarto guide](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/) covers installation and the
basics in under 30 minutes. If you already know R Markdown, the concepts transfer
almost directly.
:::

::: {.exercise-box}
### Guided task 5.2 — Your first Quarto document

1. Install Quarto (bundled with recent RStudio, or standalone from quarto.org).
2. Create a new `.qmd` file with a YAML header (title, author, `format: html`).
3. Add one text section, one code chunk that loads `data/clean/dwd_climate_clean.csv`
   and prints `glimpse()` and one `ggplot2` figure.
4. Render it (`quarto render your_file.qmd` or the Render button in RStudio/Positron).

**Reflect:** what changed in how you *wrote* the analysis, compared to a plain script
with separate comments?
:::

## Organising a Reproducible Project

Good project structure is a form of documentation in itself. A minimal, defensible
layout:

```
my-challenge/
├── data/              # raw, locked data + a data dictionary (README.md)
├── R/                 # reusable functions, if any
├── analysis.qmd        # the literate-programming narrative (or several, numbered)
├── dashboard.qmd        # the interactive dashboard
├── _quarto.yml          # project configuration
└── README.md            # what this project is, how to run it
```

This directly extends the data-management principle from
[Chapter 1](01-understanding-data.qmd#data-management): the raw download never
changes, every transformation is code and every code file has a clear place. Compare
this module's own repository structure — it follows exactly this pattern.

::: {.acemate-box}
Ask your learning buddy to critique your folder structure against this checklist and to explain
*why* a given convention exists (e.g. "why keep `data/` separate from analysis code?")
rather than asking it to generate the structure for you sight unseen — you need to be
able to justify your own project's organisation in your report.
:::

## Version Control with Git and GitHub

Git tracks every change to your files over time; GitHub hosts that history online so
others (and future you) can see it and so you have an off-machine backup. For this
module, you need a working subset of Git, not the whole tool:

- `git init` / cloning an existing repository
- `git add`, `git commit -m "message"` — saving a snapshot with a clear description
- `git push` / `git pull` — syncing with GitHub
- Writing a short, useful `README.md` at the project root

::: {.callout-tip}
## Learn Git without the jargon
[Happy Git and GitHub for the useR](https://happygitwithr.com/) is written specifically
for researchers coming from R and is the recommended path if this is your first time
with version control. Work through its "Connect to GitHub" and first-commit chapters
before your challenge deadline, not the night before.
:::

::: {.exercise-box}
### Guided task 5.4 — Put your challenge under version control

1. Create a GitHub repository for your challenge analysis (public, CC-BY licence, unless
   your data source's licence requires otherwise).
2. Commit your project in stages, with meaningful commit messages, as you go — not one
   giant commit at the end. Three to five commits across the challenge is a reasonable
   minimum.
3. Write a `README.md` that a stranger could use to understand what the project does and
   how to reproduce it, in under two minutes of reading.

**Reflect:** look at your own commit history. Would *you*, reading it back in six
months, understand what each commit changed and why?
:::

::: {.differentiation-box}
::: {.struggling}
If the command line and `git add`/`commit`/`push` feel like too much at once before your
deadline: [GitHub Desktop](https://desktop.github.com/) gives you the same version
control through a point-and-click interface — [Happy Git and
GitHub for the useR](https://happygitwithr.com/) covers it alongside the command line.
:::
::: {.deeper}
If Git already feels comfortable and you want to understand *why* it works the way it
does (branches, the object model, merging): [Pro Git](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2)
(free online) is the standard reference, far beyond what this module needs but useful
for later projects.
:::
:::

## Documentation and Open Science

Documentation is not an afterthought written at the end — it is the parts of §5.3's
project structure that explain themselves: a data dictionary next to the raw data (as in
this module's own `data/README.md`), comments explaining *why* a non-obvious cleaning
decision was made (not just *what* the code does) and a README that states the
project's purpose, data sources and how to re-run it.

**Open Science practice**, concretely, for this module:

- Publish your code and (where licensing allows) your data openly, with a clear licence
  (this module and its practice dataset are CC-BY 4.0).
- Cite your data sources properly, including dataset codes and access dates (Eurostat
  datasets are versioned and updated — record *when* you pulled the data).
- Make your dashboard and report's methodology fully traceable back to the code that
  produced it — the requirement stated at the end of [the overview](index.qmd#complete-your-final-challenge).

## Check your understanding

- Can you explain the FAIR principles in your own words, with one climate-data example
  each?
- Could someone unfamiliar with your project clone your repository and reproduce your
  dashboard from the README alone?
- Can you point to at least one commit message in your own repository that clearly
  explains *why*, not just *what*, changed?
